Imagine the gridlock when you'd need to form coalition governments like a parliament -- we'd get nothing done. The reason coalition governments work in parliamentary systems is because the legislative and executive branches are closely related. If you need more votes to claim the executive, then you form a coalition and basically have all the power. If you need more votes to be a vocal opposition government, then you form a coalition and pretty much lack power aside from yelling at the majority governmnet. Instead of more parties, we should downsize the federal government and have states pick up responsibilities, as the Founders intended. The Federal government should be supreme of course, but right now it has a disproportionate amount of power, which exasperates the negative effects of a two party system (all systems have positive and negative effects). Take the war on drugs for instance. If states determined their own laws concerning drug use, then you'd see more variation in laws around the US and more opinions represented as a result. I see your point, which is why I think we need a revitalization of the federal (little "f" is intentional) system outlined in our Constitution and described in The Federalist. Although I should mention that it's not like the parties are a cohesive unit even on the Federal level. There are factions within and between each house of Congress, and between Congress and the Presidency. And then there is the struggle between state governments and the Federal government, local governments and counties, counties and states, states and local governments, counties and the Federal government, etc. It's a beautiful system really...

You may have heard this part of Federalist 51 before: "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition," which basically means that all competing interests at every level of government compete against one another because of Madison's fundamental insight into human nature; that is, people are self-interested and will always try to make their opinion heard. This is the basic "I took a class on the Constitution!" understanding, but there is still more. I can't say it any better than Madison, so here you go:

"Ambition must be made to counteract ambition. The interest of the man must be connected with the constitutional rights of the place. It may be a reflection on human nature, that such devices should be necessary to control the abuses of government. But what is government itself, but the greatest of all reflections on human nature? If men were angels, no government would be necessary. If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on government would be necessary. In framing a government which is to be administered by men over men, the great difficulty lies in this: you must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself."

The constitutional right of the place referenced here is literally the person's capacity in government. Senators will try to maximize the power of the Senate, Presidents will try to maximize executive power, etc. Now there are certainly executions to this rule, which we call acts of statesmanship. For instance, Washington choosing to leave office after two terms is an example of excellent statesmanship. But Madison recognized that not everybody will be George Washington, and so competing interests must be unleashed to ensure that no single person or party can become tyrannical. In the process, the incredible plethora of opinions that make up the United States have an opportunity to be heard at the various levels of government, all within a 2 party system.

It is extremely difficult to run for a major office (statewide or national) without the organization of a party behind you. That's not to say you could not construct one (Roosevelt did in 1912, Anderson did in 1980, Perot did in 1992) but the odds do not favor the approach.

Since this is voat, let's talk about voting systems! America uses a vote-for-one voting system that prevents new ideas and candidates from entering the national discussion. Game theory predicts that a vote-for-one voting system eventually turns into in a two party system. Here is an illustration of how that happens

But it doesn't have to be this way!

The necessary requirement to fix our voting system is to allow voters to express their opinion on more than one candidate.

How do we do that?

The simplest way is to allow voters to vote for all of the candidates they support. This should sound familiar because it's the same system used by the Olympics, but on a scale of 0-1.

The technical name for this system is Approval Voting, and it's how America will move forward as a country.
